extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, graduate students and researchers in differential geometry, global analysis, and mathematical physics
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic exposition of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem: definitions, hypotheses, cohomological/topological formulae, examples, extensions, and proof techniques for elliptic operators and complexes on manifolds. Presents conditions under which the analytical index equals the topological index and describes variants (families, equivariant, noncompact, boundary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability: elliptic differential operator on a compact manifold
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem applies to an elliptic differential operator D between smooth vector bundles E and F on a compact smooth manifold X (initial exposition assumes no boundary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: X is usually taken compact and without boundary in the basic statement; the operator acts on smooth sections of E to sections of F. Many of the definitions and conclusions (Fredholm property, finite-dimensional kernel/cokernel) rely on compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipticity criterion (symbol invertibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An operator is elliptic if its principal symbol is nonzero (invertible) for every nonzero cotangent vector; for operators between bundles the symbol must be invertible as an element of Hom(E_x,F_x) for all nonzero cotangent vectors at x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbol is obtained by keeping highest-order terms and replacing ∂/∂x_i by y_i; it is homogeneous of degree n. Examples: Laplace operator symbol y_1^2+...+y_k^2 (elliptic); wave operator symbol -y_1^2+...+y_k^2 (not elliptic for k≥2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical index (Fredholm index) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytical index of an elliptic operator D is Index(D) = dim Ker(D) − dim Coker(D) = dim Ker(D) − dim Ker(D*), i.e., the Fredholm index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elliptic operators on compact manifolds admit a parametrix (pseudoinverse) so are Fredholm; kernel and cokernel are finite-dimensional. Example: d/dx − λ on the circle has index 0; kernel and cokernel dimensions may jump but their difference (the index) is homotopy invariant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological index (cohomological/K-theoretic formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The topological index of D is a top-dimensional pairing of characteristic classes: (-1)^n ∫_X ch(D) Td(X) (i.e., the value of the top-degree component of ch(D)·Td(X) on the fundamental class), or equivalently defined by a pushforward in K-theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ch(D) is constructed from the symbol (difference element in K(B(X)/S(X))) and Td(X) is the Todd class of the complexified tangent bundle. Alternative K-theory-only definition uses a pushforward from K(TX) to Z via an embedding into Euclidean space and Bott periodicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main theorem (equality of analytical and topological indices)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an elliptic differential operator D on a compact manifold X, the analytical index equals the topological index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equality allows computation of analytical invariants in topological terms; consequences include integrality results (topological index defined a priori as rational is in fact integral) and the evaluation of manifold invariants (e.g., signature) as indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary conditions for manifolds with boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the manifold has a boundary, one must impose suitable boundary conditions (local or global) on the domain of the elliptic operator to ensure a finite index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local conditions (e.g., Dirichlet-type) were studied by Atiyah and Bott, but some important operators (signature operator) do not admit local boundary conditions. Atiyah–Patodi–Singer introduced global boundary conditions (attach a cylinder and require square-integrability along it) to handle such cases; Melrose's approach is referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to elliptic pseudodifferential operators
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem extends to elliptic pseudodifferential operators: symbols are more general (not polynomials) and parametrices often live in the pseudodifferential calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many early proofs work with pseudodifferential operators for technical flexibility; ellipticity is invertibility of symbol for large cotangent vectors, and the correspondence between clutching data in K-theory and symbols is useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic complexes viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: One may treat the problem using elliptic complexes 0→E0→E1→...→Em→0 whose symbols form an exact sequence off the zero section; the index theorem for elliptic complexes can be reduced to the two-term operator case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complexes with just two nonzero bundles the symbol is an isomorphism off the zero section, so the complex is essentially an elliptic operator. The analytical index becomes the alternating sum of dimensions of cohomology groups of the complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Families index theorem (index valued in K-theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a family of elliptic operators parameterized by a space Y, the index is not an integer but an element of K(Y) (or real K-theory if the operators are real).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces more refined invariants; passage from real to complex K-theory may lose information (map need not be injective). Atiyah–Singer studied families and defined pushforwards that preserve index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivariant index theorem (group actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a group G acts on X commuting with the elliptic operator, ordinary K-theory is replaced by equivariant K-theory and one gets equivariant generalizations (fixed-point contributions and Lefschetz-type formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to equivariant index formulas with terms coming from fixed-point submanifolds; related to Lefschetz fixed-point theorem analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-compact manifolds and L^2-index variants
rubrics_metrics.description: The index theorem can be extended to certain non-compact manifolds (e.g., those acted on by a discrete group with compact quotient) by using von Neumann algebra/module dimensions to obtain a finite (typically real-valued) L^2-index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atiyah (1976) developed this; kernel may be infinite-dimensional but a finite index can be defined using von Neumann dimension. Applications include rederiving properties of discrete series representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callias index theorem (Dirac operator with Higgs field on noncompact odd spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain noncompact odd-dimensional spaces carrying a Hermitian Higgs field, the Callias index theorem gives an index for a Dirac operator expressed by the winding of the Higgs field on the sphere at infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index proportional to integral of U(dU)^{n-1} over sphere at infinity; if the ambient dimension n is even the index is zero. Provides a distinct noncompact variant of index theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case computational simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: In specific geometric situations (e.g., X a 2m-dimensional orientable compact manifold with non-zero Euler class) the topological index formula simplifies (one can apply the Thom isomorphism and divide by the Euler class) making explicit evaluation easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example formula: (-1)^m ∫_X (ch(E)-ch(F))/e(TX) · Td(X) when division by e(TX) makes sense via pullback from BSO; such simplifications help compute indices in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: recovery of classical theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: The index theorem recovers and generalizes several classical results: Chern–Gauss–Bonnet (Euler characteristic), Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch (holomorphic Euler characteristic), Hirzebruch signature theorem (signature = L-genus), Â-genus integrality and Rochlin's theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete identifications: for D = d + d* between even/odd forms the analytical index = Euler characteristic and the topological index = integral of Euler class. For complex manifolds and ∂̄ the index gives Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences: integrality and vanishing properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences of the theorem include integrality of the topological index (defined a priori in Q) and vanishing results: the index vanishes for self-adjoint operators and for differential operators on odd-dimensional manifolds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: there exist pseudodifferential elliptic operators with nonzero index in odd dimensions. For spin manifolds the Â-genus is integral (index of Dirac); in dimensions 4 mod 8 it is even, yielding divisibility results like Rochlin's theorem in dim 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted proof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Several proof approaches are standard and accepted: K-theory and cobordism-based proofs (Atiyah–Singer original methods), heat-equation/probabilistic proofs (Atiyah–Bott–Patodi, Getzler, Berline–Getzler–Vergne), and pseudodifferential operator methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical development: first announcement 1963; published proofs use K-theory; heat-kernel proofs exploit trace identities and short-time asymptotics; Getzler and supersymmetry give shorter local proofs. References: Atiyah & Singer (1968), Atiyah–Bott–Patodi (1973), Melrose (1993), Gilkey (1994), Getzler (1983).
